Why a standard?

Without a consistent basis, every photograph becomes another opinion.

The world of photography was missing a baseline for asking a fundamental question: what makes an image good?

So we built the Standard in two stages — first testing the baseline across a large body of photographs, then studying how people actually perceive images.

01

Build and test the baseline.

At the time of building the engine, we tested the proposed Standard against more than 1,000 photographs to establish and calibrate the evaluation baseline.

1,000+photographs
01baseline-building stage
02

Understand image perception.

A separate perception study asked 243 people to evaluate 10 photographs through 11 questions, producing 26,730 individual responses. Those findings informed how the engine understands photographic perception.

243people
10photographs
11questions
26,730individual responses
The result: a Standard built from evidence. The Standard is not a taste preference or a single person's opinion. It is the consistent framework used to evaluate photographs and understand how a photographer develops over time.
The Standard

Six questions.
One consistent framework.

Every photograph is judged by the same six questions. We adjust for camera type and interest, so a landscape and a portrait are each judged fairly — not identically.

ONE PHOTOGRAPH

These six questions are not six separate opinions. They are six ways of looking at the same photograph.

The same photograph. Six questions.
01Difficulty

How hard was it to make this image exist?

02Disruption

Does it break the viewer's trained pattern?

03Moment

Of all the instants available, was this the right one?

04WOW

Does it take the viewer somewhere they could not go alone?

05Emotion

What specific feeling does it transmit to a stranger?

06Story

Is there a story here — and does the photograph make a stranger want to know it?

The perception study

243 people.
26,730 responses.What they revealed.

The perception study was not the same thing as the 1,000+ photograph calibration. It was a separate study: 243 people, 10 photographs, 11 questions — 26,730 individual responses designed to understand how people actually judge photographs.

One finding Story recognition varied from 32% to 92% across the ten photographs.

The same question did not produce the same response to every photograph. Perception changes with the image.
